passage:
Dear Jyoti Dadi,
I've been thinking about Sunday since I got back to the hostel. When you said, "I wish I had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet," you laughed afterwards, but your voice didn't.
I want you to know I didn't hear it as "now you must top everything for me." I heard it as a map. You showed me which silence cost you.
So here's what I did this week. I put my name down for the English debate, which terrifies me. I haven't asked Professor Rao about the research project yet, but I will by Friday. Some risks aren't worth it, like skipping sleep for marks. These ones feel like they'll let me sleep well at sixty.
Your granddaughter who talks too much,
Ankita

qa.q: What did Jyoti Dadi say she wished on Sunday?
qa.a: That she had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel hearing Dadi's regret?
qa.a: She was moved and thoughtful, noticing Dadi's voice didn't laugh, and chose to treat the regret as a map rather than a weight on her.

qa.q: Which risks does Ankita choose, and why does she skip others?
qa.a: She signs up for the English debate and plans to ask Professor Rao about the project, but won't skip sleep for marks, because only some risks will give her future self peace.

qa.q: How might Jyoti Dadi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that her words helped instead of burdened, and proud that her story is shaping her granddaughter's choices 🙂

grounding: A young woman hears her grandmother's regret about not studying and treats it as a warning, choosing which risks now are worth her future peace.

passage: Vinita, you know my Nana, the one who fixes every radio in our lane? Last month, while I was holding the torch for him, he went quiet and said, "I was good at maths, Rafiq. My father needed a hand at the shop, and I never asked if I could stay in school. I still dream about that exam hall." Honestly, my first thought was panic, like now I have to be brilliant for both of us. Then I watched him laugh at the next radio, and I thought, no, he isn't handing me a debt. He's handing me a warning. So I sorted things. Asking my professor for the lab assistant post, even if I'm rejected: worth it. Raising my hand when the group ignores my idea: worth it. Dropping out to chase something on a whim: not worth it. I want to be an old man who fixes radios and doesn't dream about exam halls.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's Nana say he still dreams about?
qa.a: That exam hall.

qa.q: What was Rafiq's first thought when Nana shared the regret, and how did it change?
qa.a: He panicked, feeling he had to be brilliant for both of them, but then saw Nana was handing him a warning, not a debt.

qa.q: How does Rafiq decide which risks are worth taking?
qa.a: He asks which ones his older self would be glad of, so he goes for the lab post and speaking up, but not dropping out on a whim.

qa.q: What might it have cost Nana to say this to Rafiq?
qa.a: Admitting an old regret may have felt painful and exposing; seeing Rafiq take it well could bring him some peace.

passage:

passage: Every Eid I, Reena, sit next to Yusuf Nana, my mother's uncle, because nobody else will and Ammi says her daughter has the patience of a stone. By the second plate of biryani he is on the same list: the partner who cheated him out of the printing press in 1979, the brother who never repaid a loan, the novel he never finished because "people like us don't get published." This year I noticed my jaw tightening, ready to say, "Nana, let it go." I didn't. I asked what the novel was about. He talked for twenty minutes, his eyes brighter than I'd ever seen them. On the drive home I felt two things at once: sad for all the years he had spent rehearsing that list, and very clear about my own. I have a half-written grudge against my old manager. I'm not going to polish it for forty years.

qa.q: What did Yusuf Nana say about why he never finished his novel?
qa.a: That people like us don't get published.

qa.q: What two feelings did Reena have on the drive home?
qa.a: Sadness for the years Nana spent rehearsing his list, and a clear resolve not to keep polishing her own grudge.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make when her jaw tightened, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of saying "let it go", she asked what the novel was about, which let Nana speak about his dream instead of defending his grievances.

qa.q: Why might nobody else sit next to Yusuf Nana?
qa.a: Others may find the repeated complaints tiring and avoid them, which probably leaves him lonelier and more bitter.

grounding: A young woman sees an older relative stuck in old grievances, listens without lecturing and resolves not to rehearse her own resentments.

Hi Naveen bhai,
Remember the empty plot behind our building where we used to play? It had turned into a dump. Plastic, broken chairs, a dead scooter. Last month I got fed up and stuck a note in the lift: Sunday 7 am, bring gloves.
I thought five people would come. Twenty-two came, including old Mr D'Souza with his walking stick, handing out bags. We filled forty sacks. The municipal van took them on Monday after Ammi and I called three times.
Here's the weird part. My marks this term are average, and nobody at school notices me. But on Sunday people kept asking, "Farhan, where should this go?" as if I knew. I felt needed. That feeling beats any rank.
We're painting the wall next month. Wish you were here.
Your cousin brother,
Farhan

qa.a: He may have felt useful and part of the neighbourhood again, handing out bags despite his walking stick 😊

passage: Why do I coach the under-tens, Sabina? Honestly, it started because my cousin dumped the job on me. I'm a very average midfielder. I've never been picked for district. passage:
"Payal, it's midnight. What are all these boxes?"
"Old textbooks, Ma. Forty-three so far."
Vandana stepped over one. "Placements start next month. You should be practising interviews."

passage: When I started going to the government school on Saturdays last year, I told people it was for my CV. That wasn't true, but it was easier to say. passage:
Ritu,
At the reunion you asked, "So what are you building these days?" and I laughed and said, "My loan repayment history." Everyone laughed. I've been thinking about it for a week.
Honest answer: nothing. I get to the office at 9:40, do the same reconciliations, eat the same paneer roll, watch two episodes and sleep. The salary is good. The flat is comfortable. Ma thinks her daughter has it all sorted. I'm not unhappy, exactly. I'm just flat. When you talked about your library project in the village, I felt something close to jealousy, and then nothing, which was worse.
I don't think I'm lazy. I work hard. It's just that everything I do comes back to me: my money, my comfort, my weekend. There's nobody else in it.
Can we talk on Saturday?
Kalyani

passage: Kishore, you'll laugh, but your question at Diwali is still stuck in my head. "What are you building, Ujjwal?" I said, "A fixed deposit." Funny, right? But here's my week. Office at ten, the same three dashboards, lunch at my desk, gym at seven, food delivery, a series, sleep. Weekend: sleep more, the mall with my flatmates. My salary goes up every year. Ma calls me her comfortable son. And I am comfortable. I'm not lazy either; I clear every target. It's just that when you asked, I saw that every single thing on that list is about me. My body, my money, my screen. Nobody's life is different because I'm in it. The feeling isn't sad, exactly. It's more like a room with no windows. Anyway. Pass the biscuits.

qa.a: "A fixed deposit."

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try as one small change?

qa.q: How might Kishore feel hearing this answer to a Diwali question?
qa.a: Kishore may be surprised that a passing question struck so deep, and want to help Ujjwal find a window 🤔

grounding: A young worker in a comfortable routine realises his whole life is turned inward and feels flat, though he works hard and is not lazy.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, Akash's older sister, and I've shared this flat with him for two years. From outside, his life looks fine. He leaves at 9:15, comes back at seven, orders the same biryani every Friday, and the salary slip he leaves on the table gets bigger each April. He isn't lazy; he has never missed a day. Last Sunday our cousin's six-year-old asked him, "What do you make at your job?" Akash opened his mouth, closed it and said, "Money." The kid lost interest. Akash didn't. He sat on the balcony for a long time without his phone, which he never does. I don't know what he was thinking. But on Monday he asked me, quite casually, what my weekend teaching class was like.

qa.q: What did Akash answer when asked what he makes at his job?
qa.a: "Money."

qa.q: What might Akash sitting on the balcony without his phone suggest?
qa.a: The question seems to have unsettled him, maybe leaving him feeling flat or wondering what he is really building, though Jahnavi can't be sure.

qa.q: What turning point does Akash's Monday question suggest, and how could Jahnavi help?
qa.a: It hints he is looking beyond his routine; Jahnavi could invite him to her teaching class once, with no pressure.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see her brother's life?
qa.a: From outside it looks fine, steady and well paid, but she notices the sameness and the long quiet on the balcony.

grounding: A sister watches her brother's comfortable, inward routine and his flatness when a child asks what he makes, noting he is not lazy.

passage:
"Tushar, stay back five minutes?"
"Did I mess up the client deck?"
"No. You fixed it." Omkar pulled up a chair. "The pricing slide. You caught the error I'd missed for two months."
"It was luck."
"It wasn't. So on tomorrow's call, you're presenting that part."
"Me? The client knows you."
"They'll know you too. I'll tell them it was your find." Omkar smiled. "Here's what took me three years to learn: always check the source sheet, not the summary. Now you know it in six months."
"Won't that make me... competition?"
"One day you'll probably run this team. Good. That's the point."
Next morning on the call, Omkar said, "Tushar found this, and he'll walk you through it," and muted himself.

qa.q: What error did Tushar catch?
qa.a: The error on the pricing slide that Omkar had missed for two months.

qa.q: What worry lies behind Tushar asking, "Won't that make me... competition?"
qa.a: He is worried Omkar might feel threatened, or that shining too brightly could cause trouble with his senior.

qa.q: What choice on the call shows Omkar mentoring without ego?
qa.a: He credited Tushar for the find in front of the client and muted himself so Tushar could present, sharing the spotlight instead of keeping it.

qa.q: How might the client see Tushar after the call?
qa.a: They'd likely see him as capable and trusted by his senior, which builds his reputation early.

grounding: A young professional shares a hard-won lesson with a junior, credits him publicly and welcomes being outgrown.

passage: When Sunaina joined our newsroom as a trainee two years ago, she couldn't write a headline under twelve words. I, Nandini, was only three years ahead of her and the only other woman on the desk, and I taught her everything I had been slow to learn: cut the first paragraph, call the second source, never trust a press note. In monthly meetings I made a point of saying which stories were her ideas. Last week she got the national desk job. I had applied too. For about an hour I sat in the washroom with a hot sting in my chest. Then I remembered her first story, on the bus depot strike, and how she had rewritten it four times. I went out and hugged her. My editor asked if I was okay. I was. What I gave her was never mine to keep.

qa.q: Which job did Sunaina get last week?
qa.a: The national desk job.

qa.q: What did Nandini feel in the washroom, and what changed it?
qa.a: She felt a hot sting at being passed over, but remembering how hard Sunaina worked on her first story turned it into pride.

qa.q: How did Nandini make sure Sunaina got credit along the way?
qa.a: In monthly meetings she pointed out which stories were Sunaina's ideas instead of letting them blend into her own.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Nandini hugs her?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel relieved and deeply grateful, knowing her mentor is glad rather than resentful 🤍

grounding: A young journalist teaches a junior what she learned, credits her in meetings and accepts being outgrown when the junior gets the bigger job.

passage:
Team lead's observation note, design studio. Vandana.
Payal (25) has been guiding our intern, Bilal. In week one she showed him her file-naming system and shortcut sheet, sat with him through two client reviews, and let him make the mistakes she could have prevented, then talked them over afterwards. At Friday's all-hands, when the bakery logo was praised, she said, "That's Bilal's concept. I only helped with the colours." Bilal now designs faster than she does on some tasks. When I mentioned this, she said, "Good, then I can learn his tricks." Next: I'm recommending Payal for the mentor programme, and Bilal will lead the next small brief with her as reviewer.

qa.q: What did Payal say when the bakery logo was praised?
qa.a: "That's Bilal's concept. I only helped with the colours."

qa.q: What does Payal's reply "Good, then I can learn his tricks" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels glad rather than threatened that Bilal is faster, and is open to learning from him.

qa.q: Why did letting Bilal make mistakes and talking them over later work well?
qa.a: He learned by doing and understood why, which builds real skill instead of dependence on Payal.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel hearing his name credited at the all-hands?
qa.a: He'd likely feel proud and seen, and more confident to lead the next brief.

grounding: A young designer shares her methods with an intern, credits him publicly and welcomes being outpaced.

passage:
Mentor's note, first-year check-ins. Vidya.
Pranav (20) came to discuss electives and ended up talking about something else. He cooks for himself now, paid his own hostel fine and chose his minor without asking anyone. But his father still pays the fees and wants weekly updates. "Am I an adult or not, ma'am? My cousin got married at twenty-one. I can't even decide if I should say I've grown up." I told him many students his age describe exactly this, and it isn't a sign he's behind. We listed which decisions are already his and which are shared for now. He seemed lighter and joked that he'd "graduated to half-adult." Next: check in after mid-semester exams; I've suggested he handle his own bank visit next month.

qa.q: What had Pranav paid for himself?
qa.a: His own hostel fine.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he asked, "Am I an adult or not?"
qa.a: He felt confused and a little behind, comparing himself with a cousin who married at twenty-one.

qa.q: Why was listing which decisions are already his a helpful step?
qa.a: It gave him concrete proof of growing up while being honest about what is still shared, so the in-between stage feels normal, not like failure.

qa.q: How might Pranav's father see the weekly updates?
qa.a: He may see them as care and responsibility, since he pays the fees, rather than as doubting his son.

grounding: A young man who cooks and decides for himself but still depends on his father's fees feels unsure whether he is grown up, and learns this is common.

passage:
Wed, late
Signed my own rent agreement today! Actual signature, actual adult. Then called Abbu to ask if the deposit amount sounded okay. So. Half adult.
Maria says she felt the same at 22: cooked, paid bills, still got her mum to book her dentist. We laughed about it at the kitchen counter over instant noodles.
The weird part was the question at Aunty's party: "So, are you grown up now?" I didn't know what to say. I earn from tutoring, but Abbu still sends money and still calls me his little girl. I choose my own subjects, but I still cry on the train back after the holidays.
Maybe it's not a switch. Maybe it's a dimmer. Mine's about halfway. That's not failing. It's just Wednesday.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz sign today?
qa.a: Her own rent agreement.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when asked, "So, are you grown up now?"
qa.a: She felt unsure and caught between two stages, earning from tutoring but still taking money from Abbu.

qa.q: What helps Dilnaz feel better about being "half adult"?
qa.a: Hearing Maria felt the same and picturing adulthood as a dimmer, not a switch, so being halfway feels normal rather than a failure.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Dilnaz calls about the deposit?
qa.a: He may feel glad she still values his opinion, while noticing she is handling big things on her own now.

grounding: A young woman who signs her own lease but still leans on her father feels half adult, and comes to see the in-between as normal.

passage:
Sunday night
Convocation photos went up. Everyone's captions have a city in them: Berlin, Bengaluru, "back to Guwahati." I have twelve browser tabs open: a job in Pune, a fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Canada, my uncle's offer at the factory. Every one of them looks right for about ten minutes. Mummy says her son can't choose a shirt, let alone a city.
Wasim called. He's joining his dad's clinic, done, decided. Part of me envied him. Part of me thought, but you'll never know what else you could have been.
It's amazing that I can go anywhere. It's also terrifying. What if I pick the wrong door and the good one closes?
Wasim said, "Pick two, give them a month each, close the rest." Closing tabs now. Hands a bit shaky.
Suraj

qa.q: How many browser tabs did Suraj have open?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Suraj have when Wasim said he had decided?
qa.a: He envied Wasim's certainty but also felt Wasim would never know what else he could have been.

qa.q: Why is Wasim's advice to pick two and give each a month useful?
qa.a: It shrinks the choice to something manageable and tests options for real, instead of freezing over twelve.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about his own settled choice?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to face so many doors, though he might sometimes wonder about paths he didn't try.

grounding: A graduate facing many careers and cities feels both excited and frozen, and a friend helps him narrow the choice.

passage: The evening bus from the district college dropped Vaibhav at the crossroads of his small town, his degree rolled up in a plastic tube. At home his sister Indu was sorting apricots on the verandah. "So, graduate sahib, what now?" she teased. He sat beside her. "That's the problem, didi. A company interview in Delhi. Teaching at the block school. Coaching for the government exam. Or staying to help Papa with the orchard." He rolled an apricot in his palm. "Every one looks good until I think about the others. Then I feel sick that I'll lose them." Indu handed him the sorting basket. "You can't eat all the apricots at once. Try one properly." He laughed, but that night he wrote the four options on a page and crossed one out.

qa.q: What was Indu sorting on the verandah?
qa.a: Apricots.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav afraid of when he says he feels sick?
qa.a: He fears that choosing one path means losing all the others, so the many options feel heavy as well as exciting.

qa.q: What small step did Vaibhav take that night, and why does it help?
qa.a: He wrote the four options down and crossed one out, making the choice smaller and easier to face.

qa.q: How does Indu see her brother's dilemma?
qa.a: She treats it lightly but kindly, teasing him and reminding him he can't try everything at once.

grounding: A new graduate back in his small town sees many possible paths and feels both excited and afraid of choosing wrongly.
